title: Infra GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules and CI/CD runbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary

This document consolidates infrastructure engineering guidance for managing the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking controls, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and operational runbooks. It's intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating GPU-backed inference capacity across Redwood's cloud accounts and private deployments.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for capacity targets, alert thresholds, and escalation steps.
- Standardize Terraform modules and patterns for GPU node pools, networking, and IAM.
- Document CI/CD pipelines for IaC changes and model-serving runtime builds.
- Define runbook procedures for common incidents (node failure, quota exhaustion, network partition).

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-platform (on-call rota)
- Document author: Asha Patel (infra-platform)
- Reviewers: Diego Martinez, Priya Rao
- Pager escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-shift-lead -> infra-eng-ops manager

High-level architecture and responsibilities
- GPU fleet control plane: infra-platform team owns provisioning, autoscaling policies, and tenancy isolation.
- Cloud accounts & networking: cloud-accounts team owns VPC setup, peering, and CIDR allocations per region and environment.
- Runtime & serving: serving-runtime team owns the inference runtime and per-node health checks; infra-platform coordinates capacity sizing.
- Observability & alerts: eng-sre owns dashboards and alerting rules; infra-platform owns alert response runbooks.

SLOs and operational targets
- Target cluster utilization: 60-75% steady-state (to allow burst buffer and failover headroom).
- Capacity provisioning lead time: new reserved pools provisioned within 48 hours for standard SKUs.
- Pod start latency SLO: 95th percentile < 30s for warm pools; cold starts expected > 30s and should be minimized.
- Alerting thresholds:
  - GPU capacity remaining < 15% of committed pool -> P2 alert
  - GPU utilization > 85% for > 10 minutes -> P2 alert
  - Node crash loop/reboot rate > 5% of pool in 10 minutes -> P1 alert

Capacity planning process (quarterly + on-demand)
1. Monthly telemetry review: infra-platform pulls 90/95th percentile token throughput, model memory profiles, and per-model concurrency metrics from Console.
2. Growth forecast: product + sales provide expected percent usage growth; infra-team translates to GPU-hours using historical tokens/GPU-hour conversion.
3. Buffer policy: maintain 20% buffer above forecast for hosted, 10% for dedicated committed pools.
4. Procurement runbook: for hardware/cloud SKU changes follow procurement checklist (contract, region availability, price-lock) and schedule change windows.
5. Communication: post capacity forecast and planned increases to #infra-announce and update the capacity dashboard.

GPU fleet topology and recommended SKUs
| Environment | Pool type | Recommended SKU | Notes |
|-------------|-----------|-----------------|-------|
| prod-hosted | shared | A100-80GB / H100 | High throughput, multi-tenant inferencing; use MIG where supported for small models |
| prod-dedicated | reserved | A100-80GB / H100 | Dedicated pools for enterprise tenants; strict isolation and reserved quotas |
| staging | shared | A10 / T4 | Cost-effective for pre-prod testing |
| private-onprem | onprem | customer-specified | Follow onprem packaging guide and FIPS/KMS requirements |

Terraform / IaC modules and patterns
- Module structure (recommended):
  - modules/gpu-node-pool: manages node pool sizing, instance template, boot disk image, GPU drivers, and node labels.
  - modules/networking: vpc, subnets, route tables, NAT/gateway, security groups, and allowed CIDR blocks for model traffic.
  - modules/iam: least-privilege service accounts, roles, and KMS bindings.
  - modules/monitoring: exporter config, metric sink, and alerting resources.
  - modules/terraform-helpers: common variables, provider configs, tagging enforcement.

- Example usage (HCL snippet):
  module "gpu_reserved_pool" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal-terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu-node-pool?ref=v2.3.0"
    name = "prod-gpu-pool-a"
    instance_type = "a2-megagpu-80g"
    desired_capacity = 40
    min_capacity = 20
    max_capacity = 80
    labels = { pool_type = "dedicated", tier = "gold" }
    enable_gpu_driver_install = true
  }

- IaC best practices:
  - Keep modules small and composable; prefer multiple focused modules vs. one monolith.
  - Enforce tagging and billing metadata in provider wrapper module.
  - Use remote state with locking (Terraform Cloud / S3 + DynamoDB) per-environment.
  - Require plan approvals for production workspaces via CI gate.
  - Lock module versions and providers in registry/source.

CI/CD and build pipelines (high-level)
- Pipelines: infra-iac (Terraform), infra-images (GPU AMI/container builds), infra-config (helm chart values).
- Stages for infra-iac pipeline:
  1. validate (terraform fmt, validate, static checks)
  2. unit tests (tflint, checkov, custom policy checks)
  3. plan (create plan, store artifact)
  4. review (manual approval for prod)
  5. apply (run apply in remote workspace or via controller)
- Protected branches and approvals:
  - Changes affecting production node pools require 2 approvers: infra-platform lead + eng-sre.
  - Module changes require at least 1 module owner reviewer and successful downstream plan in a staging workspace.

Image and driver build pipeline (infra-images)
- Purpose: produce validated GPU base images and runtime containers with pinned CUDA/cuDNN, NCCL, and security patches.
- Steps: build -> test (smoke runtime, run small inference), sign image, push to registry, update AMI catalog.
- Hardening: scan images with Clair/Trivy and block CVEs above critical severity.

Runbooks (operational procedures)
1) Alert: GPU capacity remaining < 15% (P2)
  - Step 1: Check capacity dashboard and recent growth graph.
  - Step 2: Determine whether spike is transient (inspect 1h window).
  - Step 3: If transient, notify product and monitor for 30 minutes.
  - Step 4: If sustained, trigger scaling actions: increase autoscaler max by +20% (apply IaC change) OR provision a new reserved pool.
  - Step 5: If change requires procurement (onprem or special SKU), follow procurement runbook and open ticket with sales/legal for contracted customers.
  - Owner: infra-platform on-call.

2) Incident: Node failure / crash-looping GPUs (P1)
  - Step 1: Acknowledge the alert and page infra-oncall.
  - Step 2: Isolate failing node via cordon + drain.
  - Step 3: Check node logs (/var/log/nvidia-installer.log, kubelet logs) and kernel oops.
  - Step 4: If drivers corrupted, attempt automated reimage job from infra-images. If reimage fails, mark host for manual investigation and move workloads off host.
  - Step 5: If repeated across multiple nodes, open SEV, capture dmesg and full stack traces, and escalate to vendor support.
  - Step 6: Post-incident: run failure drill, update driver installation playbook, and roll out hotfix via canary to 5% of pool.
  - Owner: infra-platform + serving-runtime engineers.

3) Incident: Network partition affecting model traffic
  - Step 1: Validate scope using ping/traceroute and control-plane health checks.
  - Step 2: If cross-AZ networking error, check cloud provider SR-IOV or VPC routing tables and peering status.
  - Step 3: Failover traffic to standby region/pool if policy allows.
  - Step 4: Communicate status to #status and contact cloud provider if needed.
  - Owner: cloud-accounts + eng-sre.

Operational checklists and run cadence
- Weekly: capacity review of hot pools, check image pipeline health, audit IAM roles for newly provisioned pools.
- Daily: verify alerts are triaged and critical dashboard panels green.
- Before deploys: ensure canary capacity = 5% of pool capacity and rollback hooks in place.

Security and compliance notes
- All GPU AMIs and container images must be signed and stored in a private registry.
- KMS usage for disk encryption and secrets required for private deployments.
- RBAC: service accounts for node agents restricted to minimal privileges; IAM roles reviewed quarterly.

Examples and troubleshooting commands
- List GPU nodes (GKE example):
  kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu=true -o wide
- Check GPU driver state:
  sudo systemctl status nvidia-driver.service
  nvidia-smi -q
- Terraform plan in CI (example):
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-terraform-state"
  terraform validate && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan

Documentation & references
- infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (detailed IaC reference)
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (previous runbook and incident history)
- infra-engineering-playbook-2026 (team norms and on-call rotation)

Change log
- 2024-11-15: Initial draft and publication.
- 2025-02-10: Added procurement checklist, updated SKU recommendations, tightened CI approval gates.

Appendix: Quick sizing example
- Given: Model A requires 40 GB GPU memory and averages 2000 tokens/sec per GPU.
- Expected peak load: 1.2M tokens/sec.
- GPUs needed = ceil(1,200,000 / 2,000) = 600 GPUs.
- With 20% buffer -> provision 720 GPUs.

If you have edits or edge cases to capture (e.g., special enterprise tenancy patterns), add them as PRs to the infra-team-wiki repo and request reviewer assignment.
